tagline: Green plains, long beaches, soccer pioneers
overview:
Uruguay is a small country on the Atlantic coast of South America, wedged between Brazil to the north and Argentina across the wide Río de la Plata to the west. At about 181,000 km² it is the second-smallest country in South America after Suriname, roughly the size of Washington state, and almost all of it is gently rolling grassland.

About 3.4 million people live in Uruguay, speaking Spanish. Nearly half of them live in or around Montevideo, the capital, a city of tree-lined avenues, a long waterfront promenade called the rambla, and an old port market smoky with grills.

Uruguay is a presidential republic with a long democratic tradition and one of the highest living standards in Latin America. Cattle outnumber people several times over, beef and soybeans are leading exports, and almost all its electricity comes from wind, water and other renewable sources. Soccer is close to a national identity.
landAndNature: Uruguay has no mountains to speak of; its highest hill, Cerro Catedral, reaches only about 514 meters. Instead the country is a wide expanse of pampas grassland grazed by cattle and sheep, crossed by slow rivers and dotted with palm groves. The Atlantic coast runs for hundreds of kilometers in long sandy beaches, lagoons and dunes, with sea lions and fur seals crowding rocky islands near Cabo Polonio and southern right whales passing offshore from July to November. Inland wetlands attract flamingos, black-necked swans and storks, and capybaras, the world's largest rodents, wallow in the marshes. The climate is temperate with four clear seasons and no extremes, and thunderstorms roll in off the plains in summer.
peopleAndCulture: Most Uruguayans descend from Spanish and Italian immigrants, with Afro-Uruguayan communities whose candombe drumming, played on three sizes of barrel drum in street parades, is a national art form. Carnival here lasts about forty days, the longest in the world, with murga groups performing satirical songs in painted makeup. Mate, a bitter herbal tea, is drunk constantly from a gourd through a metal straw; Uruguayans carry a thermos under one arm everywhere they go. Asado, beef grilled slowly over wood coals, is the weekend ritual, and chivito, a loaded steak sandwich, is the favorite snack. Uruguay hosted and won the first soccer World Cup in 1930 and won again in 1950, and the national team still plays far above the country's size.
history: The Charrúa people hunted and fished on these plains for thousands of years; most were killed or displaced during the 1800s. Spain and Portugal both wanted the land, and Portugal founded Colonia del Sacramento in 1680 to challenge Spanish Buenos Aires across the river. José Gervasio Artigas led a struggle for independence and self-rule, and after a war involving Argentina and Brazil, Uruguay became an independent buffer state in 1828. Waves of European immigrants arrived, and in the early 1900s President José Batlle y Ordóñez built one of the world's first welfare states, with free schooling, an eight-hour workday and the separation of church and state. A military dictatorship from 1973 to 1985 jailed and exiled thousands, after which democracy returned and has held firmly since.
funFacts: Uruguay won the very first soccer World Cup in 1930, playing at home in a stadium built for the tournament.
There are roughly three or four cattle for every person in Uruguay, and every cow is electronically tagged and traceable.
Uruguay's Carnival runs about forty days, the longest celebration of its kind in the world.
Almost all of Uruguay's electricity comes from renewable sources, chiefly wind and hydropower.
Uruguayans drink more mate per person than any other nation, often carrying a thermos of hot water everywhere.
